public_rationale: Substantial technology layoffs and AI-attributed announcements are documented. They do not establish the predicted job losses from an AI-bubble collapse. The antecedent remains uncertain, so the conditional-forecast rule requires not_adjudicable at this freeze. Neither the large aggregate counts nor the absence of a verified collapse-related count settles the prediction.
limitations: Announced cuts can differ from actual job losses.
Employer explanations may combine several causes.
The unstated geographic scope affects which collapse would activate the forecast.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: When the AI bubble pops, tens of thousands of people will lose their jobs.

statement.excerpt: There will be measurable damage to the stock market, but more importantly tens of thousands of people will lose their jobs and a depression will begin in the tech industry.

from_speaker: tens of thousands of people will lose their jobs
our_interpretation: The surrounding discussion makes the predicted job losses a consequence of the AI bubble popping.
The plain reading requires actual job losses caused by the collapse, rather than all technology layoffs or all cuts attributed to AI adoption.
I read the plural tens of thousands as at least 20,000 people, without treating a larger total as failure.
The context concerns the broader AI boom centered on major US technology companies, but it does not explicitly restrict affected workers to the United States.
No deadline or accumulation period is supplied.
criteria.support_condition: The relevant AI-boom collapse is independently established, and reliable records identify at least 20,000 actual job losses attributable to it, without double counting.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The relevant collapse occurs and a sufficiently complete accounting of its employment effects establishes fewer than 20,000 attributable job losses after those effects have run their course. An incomplete count cannot establish failure.
